newsitem.title: ITALY: Prodi to tell Kohl EMU scaremongering unhelpful.
newsitem.headline: Prodi to tell Kohl EMU scaremongering unhelpful.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said in interviews published on Thursday he would use a trip to Bonn to tell German Chancellor Helmut Kohl that constant reports doubting Italy's fitness for European monetary union were unhelpful.

"I intend to remind him, because he already knows very well, that this type of argument is of no use to anyone and still less to the common cause of building monetary union," Prodi told La Repubblica newspaper on the eve of an Italo-German summit.
"We all need each other -- we need France and Germany but they likewise need us. I'll tell it straight, also because I know Kohl thinks that way too," Prodi said.
Kohl, in an editorial in La Repubblica, called Italy "one of the great member states of the European Union" but steered clear of the controversy over its fitness to join a single currency.
He said he was in favour of "reinforced cooperation" -- the Brussels buzzword for allowing some European Union partners to move faster than others on some issues -- but was not specific.

Italy on Wednesday loudly denied a report in the Financial Times that EU monetary officials were working on a plan to defer Italy's entry into Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) to 2000 or 2001 instead of the planned January 1999 start date.
"There is no plan," Prodi told Corriere della Sera.
Prodi has fed Italy tough budgetary medicine to shake up state finances in order to respect the Maastricht criteria and join the single currency club at the outset.
"We will go to Bonn ready to repeat the words that Kohl has said himself," Prodi told Corriere della Sera.
"Everyone must pass the test. This is what everyone must do, including the Germans, and it's what we have to do too."
But he noted: "The criteria will be the same for everyone, but our accounts will be examined with extra-special attention."

Prodi said that as a result of the reports of an Italian EMU delay, which sent the lira spinning initially before steadying later, he had held a series of contacts with "the people who count in other capitals" confirming a will to see Italy in EMU.

"(The contacts) confirm to me that I can go to meet the German chancellor knowing that Italy enjoys full support and is in complete harmony with France and Spain in its bid to join monetary union at the start," he told Corriere della Sera.

Prodi has pegged his survival to EMU, and has inflicted unpopular tax hikes on Italians to try to ensure that this year's deficit stays within three percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), one of the fundamental Maastricht yardsticks.
Prodi said he would tell Kohl that the government proposed bringing forward its 1998 budget to try to banish doubts about Italy's determination to respect the Maastricht criteria.

The government is already evaluating whether to pass a mini-budget. Analysts estimate it would need to be in the order of 25 trillion lire ($15 billion) to plug a hole in state accounts caused by an overshoot in the 1996 public sector borrowing requirement.
Prodi has said he will decide after official state accounts are published at the end of February or the start of March.
"We will evaluate this within the next few weeks or months," he told La Repubblica. ($ = 1622 Italian Lire)
